definition: Pedantic means overly focused on minor rules and details, often to show off knowledge.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word pedantic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know pedantic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The wine club's newest member turned every toast pedantic, pausing mid-sip to correct the vintage by a single year.
A careful proofreader catches what matters and stops there; pedantic strictness drifts past that point — off the work itself and onto trifling rules, with the reader left behind.
An exacting reviewer demands much but honestly serves the work; pedantic goes further — the demands drift to the smallest rules, and the point quietly becomes the demonstrator's own learning.

Nitpicking faults every small thing it can reach — a comma here, a rounding error there — but it stays a habit of criticism. Pedantic behavior needs a further ingredient: the parade of learning — details policed chiefly so the expert's knowledge gets seen.

Hairsplitting draws distinctions too fine to matter — differences real only under a magnifying glass. A pedantic performance often splits hairs, but the word adds a motive: minor rules pressed on an audience mainly to show off what the presser knows.

untroubled by minor slips

Pedante came into English essentially sealed: its own small family — pedant, pedantry, pedantic — is the whole household. Its deeper Italian ancestry is genuinely debated (one guess connects it to the Greek for 'child-leading,' the root behind pedagogue, but scholars have never settled it), so there is no confirmed cousin to point to.
Pedantic means overly focused on minor rules and details, often to show off knowledge.
The hiking club's message board asked a simple question: which trailhead has parking?

Its resident expert answered in nine paragraphs — the surveyed elevation of each lot to the decimal, the Forest Service's numbering conventions since 1962, and a closing correction of the asker's spelling of 'chaparral.' The parking question died somewhere in paragraph two.
That performance — knowledge deployed to show itself off on details nobody needed — is pedantic in full flower.
Pedantic is the exact word because it captures both halves: minor rules and details, plus the showing off.
An exacting editor sweats details in service of the work; the pedant sweats them in service of being seen knowing.
The tell is the audience — the exacting writer keeps the reader in mind; the pedant keeps the mirror.
Pedantic is never praise: it says the details have stopped serving the work and started serving the speaker.
Reach for it when someone polices trifles to show off learning — and notice what it is not: an exacting surgeon or a careful auditor is paid precisely for that rigor.
The pedant's rigor is unpaid, unasked for, and aimed at an audience.

The trail club's new guide knew more botany than the rest of us combined, and he made sure we felt it.
At the first switchback he halted the line to set right a hiker who had called a fir a pine, then spelled the Latin name twice, slowly, for anyone taking notes.
By noon the lecture had swallowed the hike.
We covered half the planned distance because no wildflower could be passed until its family, genus, and discoverer had been recited.
Nobody doubted his knowledge.
What wore the group down was the pedantic insistence that every trifling label be gotten exactly right, whether or not anyone had asked.
On the drive home, someone said quietly that she had learned forty names and nothing about the mountain.
